source_text: Εἶδον ἐν τοῖς κάτω μέρεσι, κολάσεως μὲν βάραθρον τοὺς δυσσεβεῖς δεχόμενον, εὐσεβέσι δὲ χῶρον ἕτερον ἀνειμένον. Ἐλογισάμην δὲ πάντα ὅμοια ὑπάρχειν παρὰ Θεῷ νομίζεσθαι καὶ κρίνεσθαι, ταυτὸν εἶναι δικαίους καὶ ἀδίκους, λογικὰ καὶ ἄλογα. Χρόνον τε γὰρ ἅπασιν ὁμοίως ἐπιμεμετρῆσθαι, καὶ θάνατον ἐπηρτῆσθαι, ταυτόν τε εἶναι παρὰ Θεῷ κτηνῶν τε καὶ ἀνθρώπων φῦλα, διαφέρειν δὲ ἀλλήλων, μόνῳ τῷ ἐνάρθρῳ τῆς φωνῆς· συμβαίνειν δὲ αὐτοῖς ἅπαντα παραπλήσια, καὶ τὸν θάνατον χωρεῖν, οὐδὲν μᾶλλον ἐπὶ τὰ λοιπὰ τῶν ζώων, ἤπερ καὶ ἐπ᾽ ἀνθρώπους. Πνεῦμα γὰρ πᾶσιν ὅμοιον εἶναι, καὶ πλέον ὑπάρχειν ἐν ἀνθρώποις μηδέν, ἀλλὰ πάντα ἑνὶ λόγῳ εἶναι μάταια, ἀπὸ τῆς αὐτῆς γῆς λαβόντα τὴν σύστασιν, καὶ εἰς τὴν αὐτὴν γῆν ἕξοντα τὴν ἀνάλυσιν. Ἄδηλον γὰρ εἶναι περί τε τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων ψυχῶν, εἰ ἀναπτήσονται ἄνω, καὶ περὶ τῶν λοιπῶν ἃς τὰ ἄλογα κέκτηνται, εἰ κάτω διαρρυήσονται. Καὶ ὅ μοι ἐδόκει μηδὲν ἕτερον ὑπάρχειν ἀγαθόν, εἰ μὴ τρυφὴ καὶ τῶν παρόντων χρῆσις. Οὐ γὰρ εἶναι πάλιν ᾠήθην, ἐπὶ τὴν ἀπόλαυσιν τούτων ἐλθεῖν δυνατόν, ἅπαξ ἀνθρώπῳ θανάτου γευσαμένῳ.
thought_title: Judgment below, and the reasoning that man is no better than a beast
orientation: Solomon sees judgment below, then recalls his former reasoning that human beings are no better than beasts.
pass_a_gloss: I saw in the lower parts a pit of punishment receiving the impious, and for the pious another place set apart, dedicated. And I reckoned that all things are alike to be considered and judged before God; that righteous and unrighteous are the same, rational and irrational beings. For (I reckoned) that time has been measured out to all alike, and death has been hung over them, and that the tribes of cattle and of men are the same before God, and differ from one another only in the articulateness of the voice; and that all things happen to them nearly alike, and death advances no more upon the rest of the living creatures than also upon men. For (I reckoned) that breath, spirit is alike for all, and nothing more exists in men, but all things in one word are vain, having taken their constitution from the same earth, and going to have their dissolution into the same earth. For (I reckoned) that it is unclear concerning the human souls, whether they will fly up upward, and concerning the rest, which the irrational ones possess, whether they will flow away downward. And so it seemed to me that no other good exists except luxury and the use of present things. For I supposed that it is not possible to come again to the enjoyment of these things, for a man having once tasted death.

pass_b_english: I saw in the regions below a pit of punishment receiving the ungodly, and another place set apart for the godly (Ecclesiastes 3:16-17).

And I reasoned that before God all things were regarded and judged alike: that the righteous and the unrighteous were the same, and so were creatures with reason and creatures without it (Ecclesiastes 3:18). For, I thought, a span of time was measured out to all alike, and death hung over them; before God the races of beasts and of human beings were the same, and they differed from one another only in articulate speech; everything befell them in much the same way, and death came no more to the other living creatures than to human beings (Ecclesiastes 3:19). All, I supposed, had the same breath, and human beings had nothing more (Ecclesiastes 3:19); in a word, all things were empty, taking their make-up from the same earth and bound to be dissolved into the same earth (Ecclesiastes 3:20). For it was uncertain, I thought, whether human souls would fly upward, and whether the other souls, those that beasts possess, would melt away downward (Ecclesiastes 3:21).

And so it seemed to me that there was no other good than pleasure and the use of what is at hand (Ecclesiastes 3:22). For I supposed that once a human being has tasted death, he cannot come back again to the enjoyment of these things (Ecclesiastes 3:22).
notes: Paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 3:16-22. Everything after the first sentence is in indirect speech governed by ἐλογισάμην ('I reasoned') and ᾠήθην ('I supposed'): it reports the speaker's former mistaken reasoning, not Gregory's settled view (he answers it in the next sections and in chapter 9). The English keeps that frame with 'I reasoned', 'I thought', 'I supposed' and past tense, and does not turn it into a plain statement. 'Breath' renders πνεῦμα, following the sense of Ecclesiastes 3:19 (πνεῦμα ἓν τοῖς πᾶσιν); 'spirit' is also possible. 'The regions below' (ἐν τοῖς κάτω μέρεσι) replaces the verse's 'under the sun'; Gregory reads the place of judgment as the underworld. καὶ ὅ μοι ἐδόκει at the start of the last paragraph is awkward Greek (ὅ without a clear antecedent); read as 'and so it seemed to me'. 'Pleasure' renders τρυφή (luxury, indulgence). The last sentence answers 3:22b ('who will bring him to see what will be after him?').
